title: Live-Dead-Live Verification of Absence of Voltage

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Training room ceiling grid with a locked-out 277 V troffer overhead; a ladder set up beneath it, lock and tag visible on a breaker panel in the background. Medium shot of Matthew beside the ladder.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: Test Before You Touch
scenes.says: Before you open this fixture, think about what could hurt you. The big one is a circuit you think is dead that isn't. So the plan starts at the shop: your meter, spare leads and battery, a proving unit, your PPE and a supervisor lined up. Lock out first, then test. Know what you'll do if a reading surprises you, before it happens.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Same location. Close-up of a breaker with a lock and tag applied, then a printed panel schedule.
scenes.on_screen: Locking out is not enough by itself
scenes.says: Locking out a breaker is not enough by itself. The panel schedule might be wrong. The fixture might be fed by two circuits. Someone might have back-fed it. Or your meter might be broken. The only way to know a conductor is safe is to test it with a working meter at the point of work.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew at a whiteboard with three boxes drawn: LIVE, DEAD, LIVE.
scenes.on_screen:
1. LIVE - prove the meter
2. DEAD - test every conductor
3. LIVE - prove the meter again
scenes.says: OSHA requires that you check your tester immediately before and immediately after the test. NFPA 70E describes the same process. We call it live-dead-live. Live: prove the meter on a known source. Dead: test all conductors at the work location. Live again: re-test on the same source. If the meter fails that last check, your dead reading means nothing.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech performs the steps at the locked-out training troffer, in required PPE, with a qualified supervisor standing beside the ladder; presenter voice-over. Real-time, uncut take.
scenes.on_screen: Safety: Until verified, treat conductors as energized. At LT1: training, PPE and direct supervision of a qualified person.
scenes.says: Until absence of voltage is verified, the conductors are considered energized. OSHA and NFPA 70E assign this test to a qualified person. At LT1, you perform it only after training, wearing the PPE required by our electrical safety program, and under the direct supervision of a qualified person until the company documents that you're qualified for this task.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech performs the steps; presenter voice-over. Close-ups of meter inspection, leads going into COM and V, dial turned to AC volts, then the meter probes on a proving unit.
scenes.on_screen: Black lead: COM | Red lead: V | Dial: AC volts
scenes.says: Watch the order. Before starting, the circuit is locked and tagged, the switch has been tried and is back off. He inspects the meter and leads. Black lead in COM, red lead in V, dial on AC volts. PPE on. Now the first live check, on a proving unit, a small battery device that makes a test voltage right at the work location. Correct reading. The meter works.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech opens the fixture without touching conductors and tests each combination; presenter voice-over. Caption updates with each test point.
scenes.on_screen:
Hot to neutral
Hot to ground
Neutral to ground
(Two-hot circuits: each hot to ground, hot to hot)
scenes.says: He opens the fixture carefully and doesn't touch the conductors. On this single-phase 277 volt circuit he tests hot to neutral, hot to ground, and neutral to ground. Each should read zero or a fraction of a volt. He also tests any other conductors in the box: switch legs, travelers, other circuits. On a 208 or 480 volt two-hot circuit, you test each hot to ground and hot to hot.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech re-tests the meter on the same proving unit; presenter voice-over. Close-up of the reading.
scenes.on_screen: Re-prove the meter. Only now is it de-energized.
scenes.says: Now, immediately, the second live check, on the same proving unit. Correct reading. Only now is this fixture considered de-energized for your work. Remember, proving on a 120 volt receptacle checks the meter, but for 277 volts, a 277 volt source or a proving unit that covers the range is better.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Second clip: same troffer. The meter shows 277 V on what should be a dead circuit. Senior tech lowers the probes, steps down and back, raises a hand to keep others away, and calls the supervisor.
scenes.on_screen: Unexpected voltage? STOP. Step back. Call your supervisor.
scenes.says: Here's the clip nobody wants to live. The circuit is locked out and the meter reads 277. Wrong breaker, a second circuit, a backfeed. It doesn't matter which. Stop. Step back, keep others away and notify your supervisor. A few volts to tens of volts? Also stop. A qualified person evaluates it. And if the meter reads nothing on the live check, fix the meter and start over.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew at the training troffer, holding the white neutral conductor's wire nut up for camera (de-energized prop); emergency battery pack visible inside an open fixture.
scenes.on_screen: A white wire is not automatically safe
scenes.says: A common mistake: trusting the white wire. In multiwire branch circuits and miswired systems, a neutral can carry current from another circuit. Open it and you can become part of the circuit. Also check for emergency battery packs, generator or inverter-fed circuits, three-way switching, and capacitors in older HID and fluorescent fixtures. Wait as the label directs.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew facing camera, medium shot, training room.
scenes.on_screen: Never trust a breaker, a label or a sniffer alone.
scenes.says: So never trust a breaker, a label or a non-contact tester alone. Prove the meter, test every combination, prove the meter again. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Scenes 4-7 should be filmed as one real-time, uncut take at a genuinely locked-out 277 V training troffer, with the performing tech in the PPE required by the company electrical safety program and a qualified supervisor visible in frame. Props: CAT-rated DMM with leads, proving unit, lock and tag, ladder, open troffer with hot, neutral and ground identifiable. Scene 8 is staged: show the 277 V display as an insert shot on a de-energized setup or proving unit; never stage it on a live open fixture. Scene 9 prop: open fixture with an emergency battery pack.
